\[
x_k = \rho\, x_{k-1} + w_k,\quad y_k = x_k + v_k,\qquad
K_k = \frac{P_k^-}{P_k^- + \sigma_v^2},\quad \hat{x}_k = \hat{x}_k^- + K_k\,(y_k - \hat{x}_k^-),\qquad
\hat{x}_k^{s} = \hat{x}_k + \frac{\rho P_k}{P_{k+1}^-}\,(\hat{x}_{k+1}^{s} - \hat{x}_{k+1}^-)
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(y_k\): The pixel, with the image mean taken off
- \(x_k\): The clean value
- \(\rho\): The correlation of neighboring values
- \(\sigma_v\): The noise sigma
- \(P_k^-, P_k\): The variance of the prediction and of the estimate
- \(K_k\): The Kalman gain
- \(\hat{x}_k^{s}\): The smoothed estimate

Along a row, the clean value x follows a first-order autoregressive model with correlation rho. Each pixel y adds white noise v of variance sigma_v^2. The prediction is x_k^- = rho x_(k-1). Its variance is P_k^- = rho^2 P_(k-1) + q, with q = sigma_x^2 (1 - rho^2). The Kalman gain K weighs the prediction against the pixel. The Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother then runs back along the row, so each estimate also uses the pixels after it. Rho and the signal variance sigma_x^2 come from the image. The signal variance is the variance of the lines minus the noise variance. Rho comes from the covariance of neighbors, which white noise does not change. The columns of the noisy image get their own model and run, and the result is the mean of the row and column runs. This separable form is PixelNexus's own.
